subject: How to create some triangular matrix ?

messages.author: bcfb6bc9f75aae0f
messages.subject: How to create some triangular matrix ?
parts:
Dear list,

I want to create a set of N simplexes parameters S[j], j in 1..n, of size j ; more graphically, and equivalently, I want to create an upper triangular NxN matrix M with the constraints :
  • M[1,1]=1
  • for all i in 2..N, M[i,1]=0
  • for all j in 2..n :
    • for all i in 1..i : M[i,j]>=0
    • sum(M[i,j],i=1,j)=1
    • for all i in j+1..n : M[i,j]=0

I wish I could express that (in "pseudo-Stan") as
for (j in 1:N) {
    simplex[j] M[1:j];
}

I could live with a "vector of vectors" such as :
for ( i in 1:N) {
    simplex[i] M[i]
}
 and access the elements with M[i][j], but, as fart as I know, nothing of this is legal Stan.

How would you express this idea ?

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to create some triangular matrix ?
parts:
I'm guessing you want to do some kind of mixture of mixtures
and the M here are the mixing probabilities. Sadly, we don't
have a clean way to code that.

So far, like BUGS and JAGS, all the data structures in Stan
are both dense and rectangular. So there's no way to
create a single data structure of the kind you want. If
you want to enforce the simplex constraint and Jacobian yourself
and leave a bunch of the M data structure empty, that you could
do, but it's not going to be pretty (though the simplex constraint
can be folded into a function).

My next really big project is going to be to deal with sparse
and ragged structures. So hopefully some time later in 2017. But
even then, I don't know if I'll manage to handle ragged arrays of
simplexes.

- Bob

Le mardi 22 novembre 2016 à 16:44 -0500, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
> I'm guessing you want to do some kind of mixture of mixtures
> and the M here are the mixing probabilities.

Close, but no cigar :-). (A lollipop ?)

Sorry to be so imprecise : the idea does belong to me, but this is (as
always in science) a collaboration, and I do not (yet) have the
approval of all the participants to share it : some of them fear undue
competition.

> Sadly, we don't
> have a clean way to code that.

The ability to use structures of types specified at runtime is one of
the key points of C++'s intricacies (as well as a strong point of
"weakly typed" languages such as Lisp, R or, to some degree, Python).

That's one feature of C++ that Stan should keep or emulate. The
obsession of statisticians with vectors, matrices and arrays is
somewhat unhealthy : it is difficult and "unnatural" to use them to
represent "sparse" or "irregular" suructures, such as the graphs that
are a "natural" representation of correlation (or causality)
structures.

>
> So far, like BUGS and JAGS, all the data structures in Stan
> are both dense and rectangular.  So there's no way to
> create a single data structure of the kind you want.  If
> you want to enforce the simplex constraint and Jacobian yourself
> and leave a bunch of the M data structure empty, that you could
> do, but it's not going to be pretty (though the simplex constraint
> can be folded into a function).
That's what I was afraid of. Sigh...

>
> My next really big project is going to be to deal with sparse
> and ragged structures.  So hopefully some time later in 2017.  But
> even then, I don't know if I'll manage to handle ragged arrays of
> simplexes.

A Lisp-like list type with unspecified (or run-time specified) content,
or even a vector of unspecified (or runtime-specified) content (à la
Python list) would be a good start.

After all, C manages that quite efficiently (and sloppily) with
pointers, pointers to pointers, pointers to pointers to... You know the
drill. And Lisp is even more parsimonious (and elegant (and sloppy))
with exactly one data structure to do all of this.

(And yes, I know the drill of debugging the messes so easily created.
Memory allocation and management is not fun... At least, Lisp manages
*that*).

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

>> and the M here are the mixing probabilities.
>
> Close, but no cigar :-). (A lollipop ?)
>
> Sorry to be so imprecise : the idea does belong to me, but this is (as
> always in science) a collaboration, and I do not (yet) have the
> approval of all the participants to share it : some of them fear undue
> competition.
>
>> Sadly, we don't
>> have a clean way to code that.
>
> The ability to use structures of types specified at runtime is one of
> the key points of C++'s intricacies (as well as a strong point of
> "weakly typed" languages such as Lisp, R or, to some degree, Python).
>
> That's one feature of C++ that Stan should keep or emulate.

I'm not sure what you mean by feature of C++.

If you define an array in C++ (or in C), it's rectangular.

If you use the Eigen matrix library in C++, the matrices
and vectors are dense. They have a sparse matrix library,
but it's not as complete and it's *much* slower. The obsession
computer scientists have with rectangular structures is that
it allows us to control memory locality and blocking in order
to write these efficient matrix operations.

If you use the vector class in the standard C++ library,
you do get ragged structures, but you don't get efficient,
low-memory structures with guaranteed memory locality.

So it's all a tradeoff, as usual.

> The
> obsession of statisticians with vectors, matrices and arrays is
> somewhat unhealthy : it is difficult and "unnatural" to use them to
> represent "sparse" or "irregular" suructures, such as the graphs that
> are a "natural" representation of correlation (or causality)
> structures.

I only play a statistician on this list.

As you may have noticed in my last message, I said I'd be
working on adding sparse and ragged structures. They're
also much harder to work with on the code side, which is why
I can't bang them out in a weekend.

>> So far, like BUGS and JAGS, all the data structures in Stan
>> are both dense and rectangular. So there's no way to
>> create a single data structure of the kind you want. If
>> you want to enforce the simplex constraint and Jacobian yourself
>> and leave a bunch of the M data structure empty, that you could
>> do, but it's not going to be pretty (though the simplex constraint
>> can be folded into a function).
>
> That's what I was afraid of. Sigh...
>
>>
>> My next really big project is going to be to deal with sparse
>> and ragged structures. So hopefully some time later in 2017. But
>> even then, I don't know if I'll manage to handle ragged arrays of
>> simplexes.
>
> A Lisp-like list type with unspecified (or run-time specified) content,
> or even a vector of unspecified (or runtime-specified) content (à la
> Python list) would be a good start.
Not going to happen on my watch.

> After all, C manages that quite efficiently (and sloppily) with
> pointers, pointers to pointers, pointers to pointers to...

No! It's not efficient at all. It might seem that way compared
to R or python, but it's terrible from a CPU perspective.
Specifically, it destroys memory locality, introducing "pointer chasing",
which can take an order of magnitude longer than an arithmetic operation
even on a machine with fast memory. Wherever possible, optimizing
compilers will unfold this chase statically at compile time (inlining,
etc.), but if you make it dynamic, you're hosed. And making it
really dynamic in terms of type is what makes R and Python so slow
in their interpreted forms.

It also loses type safety because a pointer is just a pointer to
memory.

> You know the
> drill.

Sadly, I do.

> And Lisp is even more parsimonious (and elegant (and sloppy))
> with exactly one data structure to do all of this.
And even less efficient.

> (And yes, I know the drill of debugging the messes so easily created.
> Memory allocation and management is not fun... At least, Lisp manages
> *that*).

Memory allocation isn't the issue (it's an issue, but that's not why
pointers are avoided in modern C++ libraries like Boost and Eigen---it's
the fact that they require pointer-chasing at run time---it's the same
reason templates are preferred over OO).

We're managing dynamic memory in C++ through operator new abstractions
for reverse-mode autodiff and RAII patterns for other memory (following
both the std::vector and Eigen::Matrix pattern).

And we take code contributions and are happy to welcome new contributors!

- Bob

messages.author: bcfb6bc9f75aae0f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How to create some triangular matrix ?
parts:
Dear Bob,

I agree that there is a tradeoff between expressivity and efficiency (which is, of course, a special aspect of the general tradeoff between competence and performance).

I also agree that the nature of MCMC computations tips the scales very heavily in favor of performance. (and, yes, I understand that a general-purpose Lisp-like list isn't efficient (linear access time...)). In my case, the scale has just been tipped a bit too far...

But a vector-of-vectors *can* be accessed efficiently : it "just" needs a *different* accessor, that offsets its index. *That* should be implemented.

As for implementing it myself : Heavens ! My performance in C++ is abysmal.

For my problem : I think that, in current Stan, I can neglect that M[1,1]==1 constant create auxilliary functions translating (row-column) adresses in M to linear adresses in a vector and back, and declare a vector of parameters :
vector<min=0,max=1>[n*(n+1)/2] p_raw;
and making
 p[suitable_adresses]<-p_raw[same_adresses)/sum(p_raw[same_adresses]).
That should induce Stan to take care of the jacobians. Finding the prior distribution on p_raw giving the "right" Dirichlet prior to p is probably somewhere in the literature, but, in my case, I can also go with a
p_raw~uniform(0,1)
without being far from the truth... which spares me to add anything to the log-posterior for these priors. Yay !
Only problem : force initialization to non-zero values, to avoid sum(p_raw[<suitable_adresses])==0, which would cause a division by 0 exception...

What do you think ?

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

>

> But a vector-of-vectors *can* be accessed efficiently : it "just" needs a *different* accessor, that offsets its index. *That* should be implemented.

Two dimensional arrays in Stan are vectors of vectors.
You get each "row" access, but no overall memory locality.

Matrices in Stan store just the values and use the offsets,
but are stored column major. So traversing by row isn't
efficient in terms of memory locality.

We just introduced a choose(n, m) function to avoid all
the duplication of people writing n * (n + 1) / 2.

I'm afraid I didn't understand exactly what you were proposing in the way of a
function or data structure for Stan. Some kind of general tensor
structure or triangular matrix structure? We'll probably get around
to both eventually, but I'll probably take on sparse matrices and then
general ragged arrays first.

And yes, you can just normalize gamma(alpha[i], 1) draws to get a Dirichlet:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_distribution#Gamma_distribution

- Bob
